A tiny, low-stakes sample, but worth watching for whether his blistering club form carries directly into the summer with the world's second-ranked side.

Pedri.text:
Pedri arrives at 23 as the metronome of a Barcelona side he's anchored across two heavy seasons, and the numbers point to a player shifting from scorer to creator. His 2024 La Liga return was a tidy 7.62 rating with four goals and five assists across 2,808 minutes; in 2025 the goals dried up to two but the assists jumped to nine in 2,107 league minutes, a 7.54 rating that reflects deeper involvement rather than decline. The Champions League is where the dip shows, ratings sliding to 7.19, so the very top level remains the question mark.

For the tournament, the most telling line is his Spain output: a standout 8.5 rating with two goals in four World Cup qualifiers, comfortably his best work in the dataset. That international lift, behind a side ranked second in the world, matters more than three flat 2026 friendly appearances (7.1, no goals or assists). The body of work says steady, high-floor midfield control rather than a goal threat.

Vitinha.text:
A model in metronomic form. Across two PSG seasons Vitinha has barely dipped below a 7.5 match rating, and the underlying numbers have only sharpened. His 2024 was the steady-anchor version — 5 goals in 2,035 Ligue 1 minutes, a 7.56 in the Champions League — but 2025 is where his game widened. He turned into a creator domestically, laying on 7 assists in 29 league games at a 7.58 rating, then a goal threat in Europe with 6 strikes across 17 Champions League outings, again at 7.58. That blend of control and end product, from a 25-year-old central midfielder, is exactly what a fifth-ranked Portugal wants pulling the strings.

The caveat for the tournament is sample size on the international side: just 88 minutes across two friendlies in 2026, no goals or assists. But his Portugal body of work is real — three Nations League assists and a 7.68 in World Cup qualifying. The club evidence says he arrives in peak rhythm.

Ousmane Dembélé.text:
Dembélé's 2024 was the peak of a long upward curve: 21 goals and seven assists in 30 Ligue 1 outings at a 7.72 rating, with eight more goals and six assists across 15 Champions League nights. The 2025 numbers cooled slightly — 10 goals and seven assists in 22 league games, his rating easing to 7.41, and a 7.16 in the Champions League — but eight European goals is still elite output, and he chipped in across the Club World Cup, Super Cup and domestic cups too. That body of work points to a forward arriving at 28 in genuine form for the world's top-ranked side.

The flag of caution is recent and at international level: two France friendlies in 2026, no goals, one assist, a 6.95 rating, and deployed in midfield rather than as an attacker. Position matters here — his club ceiling comes from playing forward, so how France use him will shape whether that club-level threat translates onto the tournament stage.

Rayan Cherki.text:
At 22, Cherki arrives in good standing after a productive move up in level. His final Lyon season set the template: 8 goals and 11 assists in 30 Ligue 1 games at a 7.63 rating, with an even sharper Europa League return of 4 goals and 8 assists across 12 outings at 8.02. The 2025 switch to Manchester City didn't dent his creativity — 12 assists in 33 Premier League appearances, plus 3 Champions League goals and a sharp 3-goal League Cup run — even as his own scoring dipped and his rating settled to a steadier 7.20. The shape is consistent: he makes goals more than he finishes them, and he kept doing it after stepping into a stronger league.

For the tournament, that points to an assist-leaning creator rather than a primary scorer for the world's top-ranked side. France's 2026 friendly sample is thin — one goal in three games at 7.27 — so treat the international read as provisional, but the club body of work travels.

Jude Bellingham.text:
Bellingham's club trajectory tells a story of a debut-season peak and a quieter follow-up. His first Real Madrid campaign in 2024 returned 9 goals and 8 assists across 31 La Liga games at a 7.48 rating, with a further 3 goals and 3 assists in the Champions League. The 2025 numbers cooled: 6 goals and 4 assists in 28 league outings at 7.28, and a 7.2 rating across nine European nights. The output dropped, even if the floor stayed high.

What lifts the read for the tournament is the England version of him. He scored and created at the Euros (7.44) and was outstanding in the Nations League, rating 8.33 while deployed as an attacker rather than a deeper midfielder. His early 2026 work is thin but tidy — an assist and a 7.6 in World Cup qualifying. At 22 and ranked behind a fourth-placed side, he profiles as a player whose club returns understate his international ceiling, particularly when pushed higher up the pitch.

Unai Simón.text:
The numbers paint Unai Simón as a dependable rather than spectacular presence, and a heavily used one. His club workload jumped from 25 La Liga appearances in 2024 to a full 37 across 3,330 minutes in 2025, a near-ever-present season that nudged his domestic rating down only marginally, from 7.09 to 6.88. The European step-up tells a similar story: he held a 7.22 across six Euro 2024 games for Spain but managed a more modest 6.5 over eight Champions League outings with Athletic last term, with the odd low — a 4.6 in the 2025 Super Cup — dragging at the edges.

For a 28-year-old keeping goal for the world's second-ranked side, that's the profile of a steady operator who has shown he can sustain a punishing schedule. His two 2026 friendlies for Spain returned a 7.3, a small but encouraging sign heading in. Expect competence and durability rather than highlight-reel saves swinging Spain's tournament.

J. Pickford.text:
Pickford is the model's idea of dependable: ever-present at Everton with 38 Premier League appearances in both the 2024 and 2025 seasons, a full 3,420 and 3,432 minutes between the posts. His league rating has been steady rather than spectacular, sliding gently from 7.26 in 2024 to 7.02 in 2025, the sort of consistency a goalkeeper builds a tournament reputation on. Cup outings backed it up, with a 7.7 in the FA Cup and a 7.5 the season after.

The mild flag is the most recent form. Across England's 2026 World Cup qualifiers and friendlies he sits at 6.9 and 6.75, his softest stretch in this window, and at 31 the climb back to peak numbers matters. Against that, his Euro 2024 body of work — seven appearances at a 7.06 average — shows he tends to raise his level on the big stage. For a side ranked fourth in the world, that track record reads as a stabilising asset rather than a worry.

Y. Bounou.text:
Yassine Bounou heads to the tournament as a settled, in-form number one. His Al-Hilal league work has been steady rather than spectacular — 6.82 across 31 Pro League games in 2024, nudging up to 6.93 over 26 appearances in 2025 — but the pattern that matters here is how he raises his level on the big stage. He posted 7.42 in the AFC Champions League Elite in 2024 and a striking 7.78 across five FIFA Club World Cup outings in 2025, exactly the high-stakes, knockout environment a World Cup demands.

The Morocco numbers reinforce it: 7.17 over seven games at the Africa Cup of Nations and 7.33 in three 2026 friendlies. At 34 he is not declining, and a goalkeeper who consistently lifts his rating when the games get bigger is a quiet asset for a side ranked eighth in the world. For a team that may need to win matches by margins, that kind of reliability behind them is worth plenty.

M. Maignan.text:
Mike Maignan arrives as France's number one off two near-identical seasons of relentless availability: 37 Serie A starts and 3,295 minutes in 2024, then 37 again and 3,303 minutes in 2025, with his league rating nudging up from 7.1 to 7.23. That's a goalkeeper who simply does not come out of the side, and the consistency is the point — there's no dip, no rotation, no minutes lost. His 2024 Champions League work (10 games, 7.22) shows the level holds against elite attacks too, which matters for a side that expects deep runs.

The one flag is on international duty. His Euro 2024 rating of 7.33 across six games sat well above the 6.83 he's posted in three 2026 friendlies, and the 6.62 from World Cup qualifying is softer still. For the top-ranked team in the world it's a small caution rather than a concern: the club body of work is rock-solid, but France will want the tournament Maignan, not the friendlies one.

Alisson Becker.text:
Alisson's club numbers tell a story of gentle decline from a very high base. His 2024 was his strongest run, a 7.11 average across 28 Premier League games and a standout 7.62 over six Champions League nights. The 2025 league campaign softened that picture: 26 appearances at 6.78, his weakest sustained rating in the dossier, even as his European form held firmer at 7.18. The encouraging signal for Brazil is that he has rediscovered something on international duty, posting 7.18 across nine World Cup qualifiers — comfortably above his recent Liverpool league baseline and right back at his 2024 Copa America level.

For a 33-year-old goalkeeper, that mix of a slightly dipping club floor and a solid qualifying ceiling reads as steady rather than commanding. Brazil sit sixth in the FIFA ranking, and Alisson remains a dependable rather than spectacular last line — enough to keep his side competitive, short of the form that single-handedly wins knockout ties.

Diogo Costa.text:
Costa's club numbers tell a story of steady improvement rather than dramatic swing. His Primeira Liga rating with Porto nudged up from 6.98 across 32 games in 2024 to 7.07 over 33 in 2025, and the European trend follows suit, his Europa League work climbing from 6.89 to 7.05. A 7.33 mark in the Taça de Portugal hints at a keeper in comfortable rhythm rather than one being overhauled. At 26 and a near ever-present between the posts, he carries no minutes concern into the tournament.

The international samples are smaller but telling in their split. Costa graded a strong 7.34 across five Euro matches and 7.23 in the Nations League, yet only 6.6 over six World Cup qualifiers. For a Portugal side ranked fifth in the world, that gap is the one number worth watching: his ceiling on the big stage is high, but the qualifying form suggests the floor is real too.

T. Courtois.text:
At 33, Thibaut Courtois remains Real Madrid's first choice and the numbers say his level has held remarkably steady. Across the 2024 season he averaged 7.11 over 32 La Liga starts and lifted that to 7.43 in the Champions League, the bigger stage drawing the better performances. The 2025 campaign reads similarly: another 32 La Liga appearances at 6.93, but 7.29 in Europe and a standout 7.47 across six Club World Cup outings, the same pattern of rising to elite opposition. That is exactly the profile a tournament side wants behind it, and Belgium, ranked ninth by FIFA, will lean on it heavily.

His early 2026 form offers a small but encouraging marker, a 7.05 average across two friendlies as he settles back into the national setup. There is no decline visible here; if anything his knockout-football ratings are his best work. For a Belgium team whose ceiling depends on tight games staying tight, that is a genuine asset.

T. Hayakawa.text:
Tomoki Hayakawa has been a model of consistency in goal for Kashima, and the trend is the encouraging part. He played every minute he could in the J1 League across 2024 and 2025 — 38 appearances and 3,420 minutes in each — and his rating climbed from 7.06 to 7.15. The 2026 season has him rising again: 7.38 across 17 league outings, comfortably his best return and the kind of form that earns a goalkeeper a hard look ahead of a tournament.

The caveat is at international level, where the picture is thinner. His Japan minutes have come mostly in the EAFF E-1 Championship and friendlies, and his rating there (6.64 in the larger sample) sits below his club number, including an eight-minute friendly cameo in 2026. At 26 and 187cm, the profile is solid and improving, but his ceiling for the World Cup likely depends on whether that club form translates against stiffer opposition than he has faced for the national side so far.

O. Baumann.text:
Baumann arrives at 35 with a heavy recent workload but a quietly slipping line on the chart. His 2024 was his steadiest in a Hoffenheim shirt, a 7.01 Bundesliga rating across 28 games, backed by solid international cameos — 7.00 in the Nations League and 6.92 over six World Cup qualifiers. The 2025 league season was busier still, a full 34 appearances and 3,060 minutes, but the rating eased to 6.81, the marks of a goalkeeper playing a lot rather than playing better.

The flag for the tournament is the 2026 sample: three friendlies, 270 minutes, a 6.27 average that sits well below anything in his club record. It is a small sample and friendlies are friendlies, but for a 35-year-old keeper behind a Germany side ranked tenth, the trend points down rather than up. The dossier shows a dependable, high-volume career number drifting the wrong way at exactly the wrong moment, which is reason for measured caution rather than confidence.

preview.text:

The model reads it accordingly: 2.06 expected goals for the hosts against just 0.56, a 72.2% Mexico win and only 8.6% for South Africa. Mexico are favoured to open the scoring 72.5% of the time, and the cleanest outcomes on the board are 2-0 (15.4%) and 1-0 (14.5%), with both teams scoring rated a modest 38.1%.

Where the model and the market part company is on the margins of certainty. Polymarket has Mexico priced at a flat 100 cents — effectively no chance for the draw or an upset — whereas the model still leaves almost 28% with South Africa avoiding defeat. On goals the gap flips: the market sits firmly under 2.5, while the model has over 2.5 at a near coin-toss 48.8%. So treat the winner as well-signposted but not sealed, and the total as a genuinely open question rather than the formality the market implies.

review.text:
Mexico opened their World Cup at the Estadio Azteca with a controlled 2-0 win over South Africa, the kind of result the numbers had been pointing at all along. It was a clean continuation of the home side's recent form, and the scoreline landed exactly on the model's single most likely outcome: 2-0 sat top of the projected scores at 15.4 percent, just ahead of 1-0. A 2.06 expected-goals figure for Mexico against 0.56 for South Africa described this game well in advance, and the shutout chimed with a below-even both-teams-to-score read of 38 percent.

This was a good night for both the model and the market, with little to separate them. The model priced Mexico at 72.2 percent to win; Polymarket had them at 69.5 cents — close agreement that South Africa, ranked 60th to Mexico's 15th, would struggle to find a foothold. The locked bracket pick of 1-0 Mexico nailed the result if not the exact margin, and a first-to-score read of 72.5 percent for the hosts captured how the game was always likely to flow. A straightforward call, and a correct one.

Polymarket prices this as a certainty across the board — home win at 100 cents, over 2.5 goals at 100, both teams to score at 100 — where the model treats every one of those as closer to a coin flip or worse. That is not confirmation of either view; it is a genuine disagreement. The model's numbers say this is a contest the Czechs can win or draw, and the market's all-or-nothing pricing leaves no room for that.

review.text:
South Korea opened their Group A campaign with a 2-1 win over the Czech Republic in Guadalajara, turning a tight contest into the kind of narrow home victory the numbers leaned toward without ever promising. The Czechs, the more valuable squad on paper at €188m to Korea's €139m and unbeaten in their previous nine before kickoff, got on the scoresheet but couldn't take a point from the Estadio Akron.

Grade this one a clean hit for the model. It made South Korea favorites at 47.4% to win, with the draw at 27.7% and the Czechs trailing on 24.9%, and the result landed squarely on the right side. The exact 2-1 scoreline was the fifth-likeliest line at 9.1%, and with an xG read of 1.46 to 0.98 the model expected Korea to edge the goal count without a blowout — which is exactly what happened. BTTS came in too, just ahead of the model's near-coin-flip 48.6%. Our locked bracket pick, a 1-1 that called the home result correctly, also graded as a hit. A solid, unflashy night for the projections.

review.text:
Canada and Bosnia and Herzegovina shared a 1-1 draw at BMO Field, a result that quietly punctures the model's confidence. The numbers had painted Canada as overwhelming favourites at home: a 76.97% win probability, an expected goals edge of 2.36 to 0.57, and a three-in-four chance of scoring first. Instead Bosnia, who arrived unbeaten across their last six qualifiers, found the goal that turned a projected rout into a point apiece. The draw was priced at just 16.11%, and both teams scoring was rated only 39.93%, so the way this game played out sat firmly in the model's blind spot.

That makes for an honest miss to grade. The locked bracket pick was 2-0 Canada, the single most likely scoreline at 14.81%, and it landed nowhere near — the actual 1-1 ranked only fifth on the model's board at 7.58%. The market echoed the same heavy lean toward the hosts, so neither view comes out of this looking good. Bosnia's recent form, including draws with Italy and Austria, perhaps deserved more respect than a 6.92% away price allowed. A clear reminder that 77% is not 100%.

Norway carry a squad valued at nearly €590m against Iraq's €21.2m, sit 31st to Iraq's 57th in the ranking, and arrive off a run that includes a 4-1 win in Italy and a 3-1 home win over Sweden. The goal model projects 2.0 expected goals for Norway against just 0.56 for Iraq, which translates to a 71% Norway win and only an 8.9% chance for Iraq. The favoured scorelines are all clean Norway wins — 0-2 (15.4%), 0-1 (15.0%) and 0-3 (10.3%) — with the away side 71.7% to open the scoring.

Where the model and the market part ways is on degree. Polymarket prices Norway at 81.5 cents to Iraq's 5.5, materially more lopsided than the model's 71%, so the model leaves Iraq and the draw (20.1% versus 12.5 cents) more alive than traders do. The two also split on goals: the market sees over 2.5 at 60.5 cents while the model has it under even money at 47.1%. So both agree Norway should win comfortably; the open question is whether it's as routine, and as high-scoring, as the market expects.

review.text:
Norway brushed Iraq aside 4-1 in Boston, a result that flattered nobody on the Iraqi side and confirmed the gulf the numbers had flagged all along. The Scandinavians, built on a squad valued at €589.9m against Iraq's €21.2m, scored four to overshoot their 2.0 expected-goals line, while Iraq's consolation meant both teams found the net — an outcome the model gave only a 37.5% chance.

The big calls landed cleanly. The model made Norway 71% to win and Polymarket priced them at 80.5 cents; the away side delivered, and our locked bracket pick of a 0-1 Norway win nailed the result if not the scoreline. Where both views fell short was the sheer volume of goals. Five in total sat well beyond the model's expectations — over 3.5 was rated just 25.5% and over 4.5 only 11.7% — so the margin of Norway's dominance outran the projection even as its direction proved correct. Iraq's goal, meanwhile, vindicated the btts lean that a clean sheet was no certainty. A clear hit on the headline, a miss on the magnitude.

Argentina open Group J as heavy favourites, and the shape of this one is straightforward: the model's expected goals read 1.74 to 0.62, a gap that flows naturally from a side ranked third in the world with a squad valued at €782.5m facing the 28th-ranked Algerians at roughly a third of that worth. The home win sits at 64%, with the draw at 24% and an Algeria upset just 12%. That tilt shows up everywhere downstream — Argentina are 66% to score first, the likeliest scorelines are 1-0 (16%) and 2-0 (14%), and both teams to score is only a 38% shot. This is modelled as control rather than a shootout, with under 2.5 goals the marginal favourite at 58%.

Where the model and market part company is mild but consistent. Polymarket prices Argentina a touch shorter at 68.5 cents against the model's 64%, and leans slightly more toward goals, putting over 2.5 at 47.5 cents versus the model's 41.8% and BTTS at 41.5 against 38.4%. None of that is a screaming disagreement, but it's worth noting Algeria arrive in form — a 1-0 win away to the Netherlands and a goalless draw with Uruguay suggest the away 12% isn't quite a formality.

review.text:
Argentina handled Algeria comfortably in Kansas City, winning 3-0 with the kind of control the numbers had pencilled in. The clean sheet was no surprise — the model gave Algeria just a 38.4% chance of scoring and pegged their attack at 0.62 expected goals — but the three-goal margin pushed past the central forecast. A 3-0 sat beyond the model's top five most likely scorelines, which leaned tighter: 1-0 (16.0%) and 2-0 (14.4%) headed the list, and over 2.5 goals was only a 41.8% shot. So the result direction was nailed; the scoring volume ran a touch hot.

On the headline call, both model and market were vindicated and the locked bracket pick of a 1-0 Argentina win landed on result. The model made Argentina 64.0% to win, Polymarket a firmer 69.5 cents, and the favourite duly delivered without fuss. Algeria's 10.5-to-12.2% upset window never opened. This was a clean, well-graded night: the disagreement between model and market was only about how confident to be, and the more confident side was right.

preview.text:
Austria arrive as clear favourites and the numbers spell out why. They sit 24th in the world to Jordan's 63rd, carry a squad valued at €242.2m against €20.3m, and ride a run of nine wins in their last ten outside a draw with Bosnia. The model reads it as a controlled home job: 1.95 expected goals to 0.78, a 64.6% chance of an Austrian win against just 13.6% for Jordan, and a 66.5% likelihood that the Austrians strike first. The most likely scorelines cluster around 2-0 (12.4%) and 1-0 (12.3%), the picture of a side expected to win comfortably without necessarily running riot.

The market is more emphatic still, pricing Austria at 71.5 cents to the model's 64.6 — a meaningful seven-point gap that hands Jordan more hope (13.6%) than traders do (10.5%). That is the one genuine disagreement worth flagging: the model thinks the upset is slightly less far-fetched than the price implies. Elsewhere they broadly align. Both see this as a coin-flip on goals, the model's 51.4% over 2.5 sitting just under the market's 54.5%, and they all but agree on both teams to score, 46.8% to 46.5%. Expect Austrian control; the open question is the margin.

review.text:
Austria handled Jordan 3-1 at Levi's Stadium, and the scoreline tracked the favourite's profile closely. The model had built Austria up to 1.95 expected goals against 0.78, and a three-goal return delivered on the attacking edge that underpinned a 64.6% home win probability. Four goals total cleared the over 2.5 line the model rated a near coin-flip at 51.4%, while Jordan's consolation justified the 46.8% both-teams-to-score read. The exact 3-1 didn't feature among the model's top five scorelines, but the shape of the contest — Austria leading, Jordan landing one — was squarely within the expected range.

On the headline call, both model and market were right, and the market was more emphatic: Polymarket priced Austria at 73.5 cents versus the model's 64.6%, and the favourite duly delivered. That gap was a genuine disagreement before kickoff, and on this occasion the bolder market price looked the sharper of the two. Our locked bracket pick logged 1-1 as the scoreline but called the home result, so it grades as a hit on outcome if a miss on the exact numbers.

preview.text:
Portugal arrive as the obvious favourites here, fifth in the world against a 46th-ranked DR Congo, and with a squad valued at €1.01bn against €143.9m the gap in raw talent is wide. The model reads it as a controlled rather than crushing favourite's job: 1.68 expected goals for Portugal against just 0.51, a 65.8% win probability, and a most-likely scoreline of 1-0 at 18.4% with 2-0 close behind at 15.8%. That points to a side that should dominate territory but face a Congo defence that has kept its shape — clean sheets against Denmark, Jamaica and Bermuda recently, and a draw with Senegal — and may not be broken down easily. A goalless first half is rated almost as likely as a Portugal lead, 44.9% to 45.0%.

The disagreement with Polymarket is real and worth flagging. The market prices Portugal at 75.5 cents to the model's 65.8%, a meaningful gap that treats this as closer to a formality. The same split runs through the goals: the market has over 2.5 at 53.5% where the model sees only 37.5%, and both-teams-to-score at 40.5% against 32.9%. The model expects a tighter, lower-scoring win than the betting crowd does.

England arrive in Dallas as the clear favourite, and the numbers explain why. The model hands them a 1.58 to 0.69 expected-goals edge, which feeds a 58.3% win probability against just 15.5% for Croatia, with a draw at 26.2%. The squad gap is stark on paper too — €1,360m against €387.3m — and England's recent run, including 2-0 qualifying wins over Serbia and Albania, fits a side expected to dictate. Croatia, ranked 11th to England's 4th, have looked uneven lately, beating Slovenia but losing 0-2 at home to Belgium and 1-3 in Brazil, and the model sees them more as a containment side here: it makes England 62.1% to open the scoring and tilts the likeliest scorelines toward 1-0 (15.8%) and 2-0 (12.9%).

The market broadly agrees but isn't quite as bullish on England, pricing them at 56.5 cents to the model's 58.3% and nudging Croatia up to 17.5 cents. The more interesting split is on goals. The model expects a tighter, lower-scoring game — 39.6% for over 2.5 and 40.1% both teams to score — while Polymarket sits noticeably higher at 44.5 and 47.5 cents. That gap is a genuine open question: either Croatia find the net more than the model credits, or the unders are the value.

Ghana host Panama at BMO Field as marginal favourites, and the matchup carries a neat contradiction: Panama sit 41 places higher in the FIFA ranking at 33rd, yet Ghana's squad is valued at €234.6m against Panama's €34.55m. The model leans on home advantage and gives Ghana a 1.36 to 1.03 edge in expected goals, translating to a 43.6% win probability against Panama's 27.9%, with the draw at 28.6%. That points to a tight, low-scoring affair rather than a rout — over 2.5 goals lands at just 42.7%, both teams to score sits below an even split at 48.4%, and the single most likely outcome is a 1-1 draw at 13.5%, narrowly ahead of a 1-0 Ghana win.

There is no real argument between model and market here. Polymarket prices Ghana at 41.5 cents to the model's 43.6, nudges Panama up to 29.5 against 27.9, and otherwise tracks closely — over 2.5 at 40.5 cents versus 42.7%, both teams to score at 47.5 against 48.4%. The only flicker of disagreement is the away side: the market rates Panama's chances of taking something slightly higher than the model does, which fits their qualifying form. On the numbers, this is a genuinely close call best treated as one.

Colombia arrive at the Azteca as clear favourites, and the shape of this one is straightforward: a side ranked 13th in the world with a squad valued at €302m against an Uzbekistan team ranked 50th and worth €85m. The model reads it that way too, projecting 1.5 expected goals for Colombia against just 0.63 for Uzbekistan and making the away win a 58% shot, with the draw at 27% and an Uzbek win only 15%. Colombia are favoured to open the scoring (62%) and the most likely outcomes are a 0-1 or 0-2, though a goalless first half is the single likeliest half-time state at 47%. Both teams to score sits at a modest 37%, fitting a game the model expects Colombia to control without running riot.

The interesting gap is in degree, not direction. Polymarket prices Colombia at 70.5c to the model's 58%, trimming the draw to 19.5c and Uzbekistan to under 10c — the market is markedly more certain of a Colombian win. The two also part ways on goals: the market sees over 2.5 as a coin-flip at 49.5c, while the model leans under at 36%. Take the market's confidence and the over with caution; the model sees a tighter, lower-scoring afternoon.

The Czechs come into Atlanta as clear favourites, and the model's numbers back that up: an expected 1.32 goals to South Africa's 0.85, a 47.2% win probability against 23.3%, and a 29.6% chance the spread of a draw holds. The gap in resources is real, with a squad valued at €188m against €49m and a FIFA ranking of 41 to 60. The Czechs are unbeaten in nine, while South Africa arrive off two friendly draws against Jamaica and Nicaragua and a mixed Africa Cup of Nations. This shapes as a controlled European favourite against a side likely to sit deep and counter, which is why the most likely scoreline is a tight 1-0 (14.5%), with 1-1 and 0-0 close behind.

That low-scoring lean is where the model and market part ways. Polymarket prices the Czechs at 54.5 cents, materially shorter than the model's 47.2%, and sees a more open game: over 2.5 goals at 45.5 cents against the model's 36.9%, and both teams scoring at 48.5 versus 42.6%. So the market is both more confident in a Czech win and expecting more goals — a genuine tension, with the model preferring a grindier, narrower outcome than the prices imply.

Switzerland start this one as clear favourites, and the model leans into it hard: 2.06 expected goals to Bosnia's 0.62, a 70.6% chance of the win, and a 71% likelihood of scoring first. The gap in pedigree backs that up — Switzerland sit 19th in the FIFA ranking to Bosnia's 65th, with a squad valued at €332.5m against €151.6m — and the Swiss carried a strong qualifying run, beating Sweden 4-1 and 2-0 and Kosovo 4-0. Bosnia are no pushovers, having held Italy and Wales late in qualifying, but the model gives them only a 9.7% win chance and pencils in a tidy 2-0 as the single likeliest scoreline at 14.5%.

The numbers also expect a fairly low-event game: over 2.5 goals is a coin flip at 50.3%, and both teams to score sits at 41%, reflecting how little the model trusts Bosnia's attack here. The market is a touch more cautious on Switzerland, pricing the home win at 62.5 cents against the model's 70.6%, and rating Bosnia's chances higher at 14.5 cents versus 9.7%. That is the one real disagreement worth flagging — the market sees more upset risk than the model does, and with these two it stays a genuine open question.

On paper this is a mismatch, and the model treats it as one. Canada are home in Vancouver, ranked 30th to Qatar's 55th, with a squad valued at nearly €199m against under €20m, and the goal numbers reflect that gulf: an expected 3.18 to 0.61. That feeds an 86.3% home win, a 73% chance of more than 2.5 goals, and an 82% likelihood Canada open the scoring. The shape is straightforward — Canada press, Qatar try to survive — and the projected scorelines cluster around 3-0 (12.1%), 2-0 (11.4%) and 4-0 (9.6%). Worth noting, though: Canada's recent form is full of draws and low-scoring friendlies, while Qatar arrive off a grim run including a 0-3 loss to Tunisia and defeats to Palestine and Zimbabwe.

The market is more cautious. Polymarket prices Canada at 75.5 cents rather than 86, and pushes the draw out to 16.5 cents against the model's 9.8% — a meaningful gap that says traders aren't quite as sure Canada blow this open. The same caution shows in totals: the market has over 2.5 at just 55.5 cents to the model's 73%. So the direction is agreed, the magnitude is not, and the cleanest disagreement to watch is whether Canada actually run up the scoreline or grind out something tighter.

Mexico in Guadalajara is the natural favourite here, and both the model and the market agree on that much. The Dixon-Coles engine projects 1.53 goals for the hosts against 0.97 for South Korea, which translates to a 49.7% home win, 26.9% for the draw and 23.4% for the Koreans. Polymarket sits almost on top of those numbers at 48.5, 28.5 and 24.5 cents, so there's no meaningful edge on the result. Mexico arrive in form — five straight wins capped by a 5-1 over Serbia — while South Korea's recent run is choppier, a 5-0 of Trinidad and Tobago sitting beside a 0-4 loss to Ivory Coast, and the two sides drew 2-2 when they last met in September.

The closest thing to a disagreement is on goals. The model gives over 2.5 a 45.7% chance, the market only 40.5%, and it leans slightly busier on both-teams-to-score too, 49.3% against 46.5 cents. That's a modest lean toward a higher-scoring game than traders are pricing. Even so, the single likeliest outcomes are tight: 1-1 at 12.8%, 1-0 at 11.9%, with a 0-0 still carrying 8.8%. Expect Mexico on top, but not necessarily comfortably.

On home soil at Lumen Field, the model frames this as a clear but not commanding United States edge: 1.51 expected goals to Australia's 1.05, which feeds a 47.4% home win, a 27.0% draw and a 25.6% Socceroos upset. The lean rests on the obvious gap in resources — a €385.65m squad against €77.45m, FIFA's 16 against 27 — and on recent history, with the USA having beaten Australia 1-2 in Sydney last October. The scoreline distribution is tight and low-scoring: 1-1 tops the board at 12.9%, ahead of 1-0 at 11.1%, with both teams to score essentially a coin flip at 51.2% and over 2.5 priced at 47.2%.

The interesting friction is on the moneyline. Polymarket has the USA at 56.5 cents, a full nine points clear of the model's 47.4%, and trims both the draw (24.5 vs 27.0%) and the away side (20.5 vs 25.6%). In short, the market backs the hosts harder than our numbers do, treating Australia's chances as thinner than the model will allow. On totals the two agree almost exactly — over 2.5 at 46.5 cents against 47.2% — so the genuine open question here is purely how much credit the Socceroos deserve, not how many goals get scored.

Morocco arrive in Boston as the clear class side, ranked 8th in the world against Scotland's 43rd, with a squad valued at €498m to €170m. The model reflects that gap bluntly: Morocco are 65.8% to win, Scotland just 10.1%, with the draw at 24.1%. The expected goals tell the same story, 1.67 to 0.50, and Morocco's recent form backs it up — they reached this point on the back of an unbeaten Africa Cup of Nations run, beating Senegal 3-0 and shutting out Nigeria. Scotland's 4-0 friendly win over Bolivia flatters a team that lost to both Japan and Ivory Coast in March. The model's single likeliest outcome is a 0-1 Morocco win at 18.6%, with Morocco favoured to score first 67.8% of the time.

Where it gets interesting is the disagreement with the market. Polymarket prices Scotland far more generously at 22.5 cents, more than double the model's read, and trims Morocco to 49.5. The market also leans higher-scoring: both teams to score sits at 47.5 cents versus the model's 32.4%, and over 2.5 goals at 40.5 against 36.9%. So the shape is agreed — Morocco on top — but how comfortably, and how open, is a genuine open question.

This is as lopsided as group-stage football gets. Brazil, ranked 6th with a squad valued at €928m, host a Haiti side ranked 83rd and worth €55.9m, and the model reflects that gulf: it projects 3.35 goals for Brazil against 0.58, and makes them 88.3% to win with the draw a distant 8.5% and a Haiti upset just 3.2%. The scoreline distribution is a parade of clean-sheet wins — 3-0 (12.3%), 2-0 (11%) and 4-0 (10.3%) head the list — and Brazil are 83.4% to open the scoring. There is decent over-3.5 value too, priced at 55.3% by the model, with over-2.5 a comfortable 75.2%.

Where it gets interesting is at the edges. The market is firmer on Brazil than we are, pricing them at 90.5 cents to our 88.3, and shaving the draw to 6.1 cents. The bigger gap is both teams to score: the model sees 42.7%, the market only 35.5% — a genuine disagreement worth flagging given Haiti's recent form, which includes a 4-0 win over New Zealand and a 3-3 draw at Costa Rica. They can find the net, even if keeping Brazil out looks beyond them.

Turkey come in ranked 22nd and on a strong run, eight wins in their last ten including qualifying victories over Romania and Kosovo and a 2-2 draw away to Spain, while Paraguay sit 40th with a more mixed record of friendly results either side of solid CONMEBOL qualifying. That gap, plus the squad-value chasm of €473.7m to €153.65m, is why the model leans Turkey but only narrowly: home win 40.4%, draw 30.4%, Paraguay 29.2%. The expected goals tell the same cautious story, 1.2 to 0.98, pointing to a tight, low-scoring game rather than a mismatch. The single most likely score is 1-1 at 14.0%, with 1-0 and 0-0 close behind, and over 2.5 goals is only a 37.1% shot.

Where model and market part ways is on the margins. Polymarket prices Turkey a touch higher at 43.5 cents and trims Paraguay to 26.5, so it sees the favourite as the clearer side; the model keeps Paraguay live as a genuine third of the time. The market also expects more goals, pricing both teams to score at 49.5 cents against the model's 44.2% and over 2.5 at 41 to 37. Treat the favourite's edge and the goal count as the real open questions here.

The shape here is a clear favourite against a side arriving in poor form. The Netherlands sit seventh in the world to Sweden's 38th, with a squad valued at €754.2m against €406.1m, and the model leans heavily on that gap: it projects 2.1 expected goals for the hosts to just 0.96 for Sweden, and makes the Dutch 63.1% to win in Houston. Form backs the read. The Netherlands lost only once in their last ten and battered Finland, Malta and Lithuania 4-0 in qualifying, while Sweden have collapsed badly, taking only a couple of recent wins amid heavy defeats to Switzerland (1-4 and 0-2) and Kosovo. The model has the Netherlands 65.1% to score first and 2-0 as the single likeliest scoreline at 10.3%.

The market broadly agrees but trims the edges. Polymarket prices the Dutch at 59.5 cents to the model's 63.1%, nudging the draw and Sweden slightly longer in the model's eyes. The sharper disagreement is on goals: the model sees Over 2.5 at 59% against the market's 51.5 cents, and both-teams-to-score at 54.6% versus 50.5. So the genuine open question isn't who wins but how open it gets — the model expects more goals than the market is willing to pay for.

Germany arrive in Toronto on a near-flawless run, nine wins in their last ten with the only blemish a 0-2 loss in Slovakia, and a squad valued at €947m against Ivory Coast's €522m. But the gap is narrower than the FIFA rankings (10th versus 34th) suggest: the Ivorians have won eight of ten themselves, including a 2-1 away win over France this June. The model reads it as a clear but far from settled favourite's game, projecting 1.42 expected goals for Germany against 0.97 — enough for a 46.7% win probability, with the draw live at 28.1% and Ivory Coast holding a real 25.2% puncher's chance. The likeliest scorelines are tight: 1-1 at 13.3%, 1-0 at 12.4%, and a goalless draw still 9.8%.

This is where the model and the market part company sharply. Polymarket prices Germany at 63.5 cents, treating the win as close to a formality, while the model's 46.7% says it is anything but. The market also leans higher-scoring, pricing over 2.5 goals at 52.5 cents against the model's 42.8%. The two only truly agree on both teams scoring, near-identical at 48 cents and 47.7%. Treat Germany's margin, not the result, as the genuine open question.

This is a mismatch on paper and the model treats it as one. Ecuador sit 23rd in FIFA's ranking to Curaçao's 82nd, with a squad valued at €368.7m against €25.78m, and the goal model hands the favourites a 2.06 expected-goals edge to just 0.39. That works out to a 76.7% win probability, a clean sheet in most outcomes, and a 76.5% chance Ecuador score first. The form lines back the gap: Ecuador are unbeaten across their last ten, including a 1-0 win over Argentina, while Curaçao have shipped four to Scotland and five to Australia in recent friendlies. The most likely scorelines are tightly bunched around a low-scoring home win — 2-0 at 18.3%, 1-0 at 17.5%, 3-0 at 12.6% — and both teams to score is only a 28.4% shot.

Market and model largely agree on the winner: Polymarket prices Ecuador at 80.5 cents to the model's 76.7%, a modest lean toward the favourite. The clearer disagreement is on goals. The market sees this game as livelier, pricing over 2.5 at 57 cents while the model has it at just 44.2%, and BTTS at 35.5 cents against the model's 28.4%. If you trust the numbers, the value sits with the unders and a tighter, lower-scoring afternoon in Kansas City.

This is a clear mismatch on paper, and the model treats it like one. Japan arrive ranked 18th with a squad valued at €270.85m against Tunisia's €69.95m, and recent form sharpens the picture: Japan have beaten England, Scotland and Iceland 1-0 apiece, while Tunisia were taken apart 0-5 by Belgium and lost 0-1 to Austria in their last two warm-ups. The model projects 1.61 expected goals for Japan against just 0.56 for Tunisia, and makes Japan 62.6% to win with the draw at 25.3% and a Tunisia win down at 12.1%. The single likeliest scoreline is 0-1 at 17.9%, followed by 0-2 at 14.8%, and Japan are 65.3% to open the scoring.

The market broadly agrees but shades a touch more cautious on Japan, pricing them at 58.5 cents to the model's 62.6%, and nudging Tunisia up to 15.5 cents. The sharper gap is on goals: Polymarket sees both teams scoring at 45.5%, well clear of the model's 34.7%, and leans slightly over on totals, with over 2.5 at 41.5 cents versus the model's 36.8%. That leaves a genuine question over whether Tunisia find the net at all — the model expects a tighter, lower-scoring Japan win than the market is bracing for.

This is about as lopsided as group-stage fixtures get. Spain arrive ranked second in the world with a squad valued at €1.22bn against Saudi Arabia's €40.68m, and the form lines underline the gap: Spain are unbeaten across their last ten with qualifying wins like 6-0 in Türkiye and 4-0 in Georgia, while Saudi Arabia have lost five of their last ten, including a 0-4 home defeat to Egypt. The model reads it accordingly, handing Spain an expected 2.84 goals to 0.4 and an 86.9% win probability against just 2.9% for the Saudis, with a draw a remote 10.2%. Spain are 84.1% to open the scoring, and the scoreline distribution clusters tightly around clean sheets — 2-0, 3-0, 1-0 and 4-0 are the four likeliest results, which is why both-teams-to-score sits at only 31%.

There is almost nothing to argue about here, and the market agrees. Polymarket prices Spain at 87.5 cents to the model's 86.9%, with the draw and the Saudi win line up similarly close. The totals match too: over 2.5 goals is 62.7% in the model against 65 cents in the market, and over 1.5 lands at 83.5% versus 85.5. Model and market are effectively shaking hands.

Belgium arrive in Los Angeles as comfortable favourites, and the shape of this one is the classic mismatch of resources: a squad valued at €547.5m against Iran's €32.05m, ninth in the world against twenty-first. The model leans hard into that, projecting 1.8 expected goals for Belgium against 0.83 for Iran and pricing the home win at 60%, the draw at 24% and an Iran upset at just 16%. Belgium have scored freely in the build-up — 5-0 over Tunisia, 2-0 in Croatia — and the model makes them 63% to open the scoring. The most likely scorelines all favour them, with 1-0 (12.5%) and 2-0 (11.7%) leading the board.

This is not expected to be a goal feast, though. The model sits almost exactly on the fence for over 2.5 goals at 48.8%, and both teams to score is a coin-flip at 47.5%, reflecting Iran's capacity to defend deep and frustrate. The market is a touch more bullish on Belgium, pricing the home win at 68.5 cents against the model's 60% and trimming Iran to 11.5 cents. That gap is the one genuine disagreement worth flagging: the model gives Iran a little more daylight than the traders do.

Uruguay arrive ranked 17th with a squad valued near €359m against Cape Verde's €55m, and the model reads the gap exactly as a mismatch of class against organisation. Expected goals split 1.65 to 0.44, which is why the home side prices at 67% to win, against a 24% draw and just under 9% for Cape Verde. Uruguay are tipped to open the scoring 69% of the time, and the most likely scorelines are tight and one-sided — 1-0 at 20%, 2-0 at 17%, with a goalless draw still third on the list at 13%. This is a control job rather than a shootout: Cape Verde have kept clean sheets in qualifying but conceded in patches, and Uruguay's recent friendlies have been low-scoring and cagey.

The market broadly agrees on the result — Polymarket has Uruguay at 69.5 cents, close to the model's read — but the two pull apart on goals. The model sees over 2.5 at just 35%; the market splits it 50/50. Both-teams-to-score tells the same story, 29% from the model against 45% priced in. So the honest open question here isn't who wins, but whether Cape Verde find the net at all — and the model is markedly more sceptical than the traders.

Egypt arrive in Vancouver as clear favourites on paper — ranked 29th to New Zealand's 85th, with a squad valued at €116.48m against the All Whites' €34.35m — but this profiles as a tight, low-scoring affair rather than a procession. The model gives Egypt a 0.84-1.25 expected-goals edge and a 45.2% win chance, against 24.3% for New Zealand and a hefty 30.5% for the draw. That caution is everywhere in the scoreline: over 2.5 goals lands at just 34.7%, both teams scoring at 41.2%, and the three likeliest results are 0-1, 1-1 and 0-0. New Zealand's form does little to argue otherwise, with eight defeats in their last ten and recent maulings by Haiti and Australia.

Where it gets interesting is the gap to Polymarket. The market is firmly more bullish on Egypt, pricing them at 54.5 cents to the model's 45.2%, and trims the draw to 25.5 cents against the model's 30.5%. The market also leans slightly higher on goals, with over 2.5 at 42 cents versus the model's 34.7%. So the genuine open question is whether Egypt's quality simply overruns a fragile New Zealand, as the market expects, or whether this stays the cagey, draw-friendly contest the model sees.

Argentina arrive ranked third in the world with a squad valued at €782.5m against Austria's €242.2m, and the model treats this as exactly the mismatch the numbers suggest. It hands the hosts a 1.88 to 0.51 expected-goals edge and a 70.1% win probability, with Austria down at 8.8% and the draw at 21.2%.
